guides.title: The Pantry Staples Every Home Cook Needs
guides.subtitle: A short, realistic list of shelf-stable basics that turn a random Tuesday into a real dinner.
intro: We have all been there. You open the cupboard, stare at a lonely can of chickpeas and a bag of something from 2023, and order takeout. A well-stocked pantry fixes that. It is not about owning forty spices. It is about keeping a small set of hard-working basics on hand so that a handful of fresh ingredients can always become a meal.

This guide covers what we keep in our own kitchens, why each item earns its shelf space, and how to store it so it actually lasts. Start with the essentials, then add the flavor boosters as your cooking grows. You do not need to buy everything this week. Pick up a few things each shopping trip and you will be set within a month.
takeaways: Start with oil, salt, acid, and a few dry carbs.
Canned tomatoes, beans, and stock cover dozens of dinners.
A few bold flavor boosters do more than a wall of spices.
Store oils and whole grains cool and dark, and date your jars.

p: If you only buy one group from this list, make it this one. These items show up in almost every savory recipe on Bored of Toast, and with them alone you can cook a surprising amount.
list: Kosher salt: Larger flakes are easier to pinch and harder to overdo than fine table salt. Keep fine sea salt for baking if you like.
Black peppercorns: Buy whole and grind them fresh. Pre-ground pepper loses its punch fast.
Neutral oil: Canola, vegetable, or avocado oil for high-heat searing and frying.
Extra-virgin olive oil: For dressings, drizzling, and gentle sautéing.
Vinegar: One red wine or apple cider vinegar plus one rice vinegar covers most needs.
Garlic and onions: Technically fresh, but they keep for weeks in a cool, dark spot and start almost everything.

sections.h: Grains, Pasta, and Other Dry Carbs
p: Dry carbs are the backbone of quick dinners. They are cheap, they keep for months, and they stretch a little protein into a full meal.
Keep at least one long-cooking and one fast-cooking option so you are covered on busy nights.
list: Long-grain white rice: Jasmine or basmati for everyday use. See our perfect rice guide for ratios.
Pasta: One long shape (spaghetti) and one short shape (penne or rigatoni).
Rolled oats: Breakfast, baking, and even meatball binder.
All-purpose flour: For thickening sauces, dredging, and weekend baking.
Breadcrumbs or panko: Crunchy toppings and crispy coatings in minutes.
Lentils: Red lentils cook in 15 minutes with no soaking.

sections.h: Cans and Jars That Save Dinner
p: Canned goods get a bad reputation, but good canned tomatoes and beans are often better than out-of-season fresh ones. These are the items we reach for when the fridge looks empty.
list: Whole peeled tomatoes: Crush them by hand for sauces, soups, and braises.
Tomato paste: Buy it in a tube so you can use a spoonful at a time.
Beans: Chickpeas, black beans, and white beans. Rinse before using to cut the sodium.
Chicken or vegetable stock: Cartons or bouillon paste, which takes up far less space.
Coconut milk: Curries, soups, and creamy rice.
Canned tuna or salmon: Instant protein for salads, pasta, and sandwiches.

p: This is where a pantry goes from functional to fun. A splash or spoonful of one of these can rescue a bland dish in seconds. You do not need all of them, so start with the ones that match the food you like to eat.
Most of these live happily in the fridge door once opened and last for months.
list: Soy sauce: Salty, savory depth for far more than stir-fries.
Dijon mustard: Emulsifies dressings and perks up pan sauces.
Hot sauce or chili crisp: Heat plus flavor, and a great fix for boring eggs.
Honey or maple syrup: Balances acidity and adds gloss to glazes.
Fish sauce: A few drops add savory depth without tasting fishy.
Parmesan: A hard wedge keeps for weeks and grates onto almost anything.

sections.h: A Spice Rack That Actually Gets Used
p: Skip the pre-filled spice carousel. Buy small jars of the spices you will use in the next six months, because ground spices fade after about a year. If a spice smells like dust when you open it, it will taste like dust too.

Swap if you are out

sections.h: Storing It All So It Lasts
p: Heat, light, and air are the enemies of pantry food. Keep oils and spices away from the stove, even though that is where it is most convenient. Transfer flour, oats, and grains to airtight containers to keep pests out and freshness in.

Whole-grain flours, nuts, and brown rice contain oils that go rancid faster, so store them in the fridge or freezer if you do not use them often. Finally, grab a marker and write the purchase date on every jar. Future you will be grateful.

faq: How long do dried spices really last?
Whole spices keep their flavor for two to three years. Ground spices are best within about a year. They will not make you sick after that, but they lose aroma and taste.
Do I need to refrigerate soy sauce or hot sauce?
Not strictly, since both are high in salt or vinegar. Refrigerating after opening keeps the flavor fresher for longer, so we do it when there is room.
What is the cheapest way to build a pantry from scratch?
Buy a few items per shopping trip, start with the essentials section, and look at the bulk aisle for grains, lentils, and spices, where you can buy only what you need.

guides.title: How to Cook Perfect Rice, Every Time
guides.subtitle: Simple stovetop methods, reliable ratios, and quick fixes for when rice goes mushy or crunchy.
intro: Rice should be the easiest thing on the table, yet it is one of the most common kitchen frustrations. Gummy clumps, crunchy centers, a scorched layer stuck to the pot. The good news is that perfect rice is not luck. It comes down to three things: the right ratio of water to rice, steady low heat, and patience while it rests.

In this guide we walk through our go-to stovetop method for white rice, explain why brown rice needs different treatment, break down the difference between basmati and jasmine, and share a ratio table you can bookmark. We also cover how to rescue rice that went wrong, because it happens to all of us.
takeaways: Rinse white rice until the water runs mostly clear.
Use a tight lid and the lowest heat, and do not peek.
Always rest rice off the heat for 10 minutes before fluffing.
Brown rice needs more water and roughly twice the time.

p: This method works for long-grain white rice like jasmine or basmati. You need a heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid. A thin pot creates hot spots that scorch the bottom before the top is cooked.
Plan on about 1 cup of dry rice for 2 to 3 people. It roughly triples in volume as it cooks.
list: Rinse: Put 1 cup rice in a bowl, cover with cold water, swish, and drain. Repeat 2 to 3 times until the water is only slightly cloudy.
Combine: Add the rice, 1 1/2 cups water, and 1/2 teaspoon salt to the pot.
Boil: Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, uncovered, and give it one gentle stir.
Simmer: Cover, drop the heat to the lowest setting, and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid.
Rest: Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes. The steam finishes the job.
Fluff: Use a fork or rice paddle to lift and separate the grains before serving.

p: Rinsing washes away loose surface starch. That starch is what turns cooking water into glue and makes rice clump. Skip it for risotto or rice pudding, where you want creaminess, but rinse for fluffy side-dish rice.

Resting is the step most people skip. Right after cooking, the grains at the bottom are wetter than the top. Ten minutes off the heat lets moisture redistribute, so every grain is evenly tender and the rice releases cleanly from the pot.

sections.h: Brown Rice Needs a Different Plan
p: Brown rice still has its bran layer, which is great for fiber and nutty flavor but slows down how fast water gets in. It needs more water and a lot more time, usually 40 to 45 minutes of simmering plus a 10 minute rest.

Our favorite shortcut is the pasta method. Boil brown rice in a big pot of salted water for about 30 minutes, drain it well, return it to the pot, cover, and let it steam off the heat for 10 minutes. You do not need to measure the water, and the grains come out distinct and never gummy.

sections.h: Basmati vs. Jasmine: What Is the Difference?
p: Both are fragrant long-grain rices, and they are often used interchangeably, but they behave a little differently in the pot and on the plate.
list: Basmati: Long, slender grains that get even longer as they cook. Dry, separate, and fluffy with a nutty aroma. Best for pilafs, biryani, and curries. Soaking for 20 to 30 minutes before cooking gives extra-long grains.

Jasmine: Slightly shorter and plumper, with a floral scent. Softer and a little sticky, so it is easy to eat with chopsticks. Great with stir-fries and Thai or Vietnamese dishes. It needs slightly less water than basmati.
Short-grain and sushi rice: Round grains with more starch, meant to be sticky. Rinse well and use a bit less water than long-grain.

p: These ratios are for the stovetop absorption method with a tight lid. Rice varies by brand and age, so treat them as a starting point and adjust by a tablespoon or two once you know your rice. Times do not include the 10 minute rest.

sections.h: How to Fix Rice That Went Wrong
p: Do not throw it out. Most rice mistakes can be rescued, or at least repurposed into something delicious.
list: Crunchy in the middle: Add 2 to 3 tablespoons of water, cover tightly, and cook on the lowest heat for 5 more minutes, then rest.
Water left in the pot: Drain what you can, then return to low heat uncovered for a few minutes to steam off the rest.
Mushy or gummy: Spread it on a sheet pan and bake at 300°F (150°C) for 5 to 10 minutes to dry it out. Or lean in and make fried rice, rice pudding, or soup.
Burned on the bottom: Do not scrape. Spoon the good rice off the top into a clean bowl. Place a slice of bread on top for a few minutes to absorb any smoky smell.
Bland: Next time, salt the water and try cooking it in stock, or add a bay leaf or a knob of butter.

faq: Yes. Double the rice and water, but use a wider pot so the rice layer is not too deep. The simmer time stays about the same, maybe a couple of minutes longer.
How do I store and reheat leftover rice safely?
Cool it quickly and refrigerate within an hour of cooking. Use it within 3 to 4 days. Reheat with a splash of water, covered, until steaming hot all the way through.
Why does my rice always stick to the pot?
Usually the heat is too high or the pot is too thin. Use the lowest setting during the simmer and always let the rice rest before serving so it releases.

guides.title: Knife Skills 101: Chop Faster and Safer
guides.subtitle: How to choose, hold, and care for a knife, plus the handful of cuts that make everyday cooking quicker.
intro: Good knife skills are the single biggest time-saver in a home kitchen. When chopping an onion takes you two minutes instead of ten, weeknight cooking stops feeling like a chore. Evenly cut pieces also cook evenly, so your food simply turns out better.

You do not need a chef's roll full of expensive blades or restaurant-level speed. You need one sharp knife, a stable board, and a few habits that keep your fingers safe. In this guide we cover the knives worth owning, how to grip them, the core cuts, and how to keep your edge sharp. Slow down, practice a little every time you cook, and speed will come on its own.
takeaways: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one.
Pinch the blade and curl your guiding fingers into a claw.
Anchor your board with a damp towel so it never slides.
Hone often, sharpen a few times a year, and never use the dishwasher.

sections.h: The Only Three Knives You Really Need
p: Knife block sets look impressive, but most of those knives never leave the block. Put your money into one good chef's knife and add two helpers.
list: Chef's knife (8 inch / 20 cm): Your everyday workhorse for chopping, slicing, dicing, and mincing. Pick one that feels balanced and comfortable in your hand.
Paring knife (3 to 4 inch): For small, detailed jobs like hulling strawberries, trimming, and peeling.
Serrated bread knife: Saws through crusty bread, tomatoes, and cakes without crushing them.
Nice to have: A sturdy cutting board, wood or plastic, at least 12 by 18 inches. Skip glass, stone, and marble, which destroy edges.

sections.h: Set Up Your Station and Grip
p: Safety starts before you cut anything. Place a damp paper towel or thin kitchen towel under your cutting board so it cannot slip. Keep your board clear, with a bowl nearby for scraps.

For the knife hand, use the pinch grip. Pinch the flat of the blade just in front of the handle between your thumb and the side of your index finger, then wrap your remaining three fingers around the handle. It feels odd at first, but it gives far more control than holding the handle alone.

For the guiding hand, make a claw. Curl your fingertips under and rest your knuckles against the side of the blade. The knife can then glide against your knuckles, and your fingertips stay safely tucked away.

Most cutting uses a smooth rocking or forward-slicing motion, not a straight chop downward. Let the tip of the knife stay near the board and roll the blade forward and down through the food. Let the sharp edge do the work instead of forcing it.

Before cutting anything round, like an onion, potato, or carrot, slice a thin piece off one side to create a flat base. Stable food is safe food. A rolling vegetable is the number one cause of kitchen cuts.
Recipes use a handful of terms for cut size. Consistency matters more than precision, since same-size pieces cook at the same rate. Here is a quick reference.
Master this one and half your prep is covered. The root holds the layers together, so leave it on until the end.
list: Halve: Cut the onion in half from the root to the tip. Peel off the skin and trim the tip end, leaving the root intact.
Slice lengthwise: Place a half flat side down. Make vertical cuts toward the root, stopping just short of it.
Optional horizontal cuts: Make one or two cuts parallel to the board toward the root for a finer dice.
Cross-cut: Slice across your earlier cuts, moving your claw hand back as you go. Perfect little cubes will fall away.
Finish: Discard the root end, or save it with other scraps for stock.

p: A dull knife slips off food instead of biting into it, and that is when accidents happen. It also crushes herbs and tomatoes rather than slicing them cleanly.

A honing steel does not sharpen. It straightens the tiny edge that bends as you work. Give your knife a few strokes on each side every few uses. Actual sharpening removes metal to create a new edge, and most home cooks need it only two to four times a year. Use a whetstone, a quality pull-through sharpener, or a local sharpening service.

Finally, wash knives by hand and dry them right away. Dishwashers dull and chip the edge and can crack wooden handles. Store knives on a magnetic strip, in a block, or with blade guards, never loose in a drawer.

faq: What should I do if I cut myself?

For minor cuts, rinse with clean water, apply firm pressure with a clean cloth until the bleeding stops, and cover with a bandage. Seek medical care for deep cuts, cuts that will not stop bleeding, or any sign of infection.
Both are fine and both are gentle on knives. Many cooks keep a plastic board for raw meat since it can be sanitized easily, and a wooden board for everything else.
How do I know when my knife needs sharpening?
Try slicing a ripe tomato or a sheet of paper. If the blade slides off the tomato skin or tears the paper instead of cutting cleanly, it is time.

p: Bored of Toast is a small, free recipe website. We do not ask you to create an account, and we do not sell your personal information. This page explains, in plain English, what little information is involved when you visit our site and what we do with it.
By using Bored of Toast, you agree to the practices described here. If you have any questions, you can always reach us at hello@boredoftoast.com.

Our contact form works by opening your own email app with a pre-filled message to us. We do not store form entries on our servers. When you send that email, we receive your email address, your name if you include it, and whatever you write.
We use this only to read and reply to your message. We will not add you to a mailing list or share your email with anyone else without asking you first.
If we launch a newsletter in the future, it will be strictly opt-in, and every email will include a simple way to unsubscribe.
